Shattered windows, wrecked cars and a blast crater marked the aftermath of a Russian bombardment in Kyiv, on Thursday 19 November 2026. The strikes damaged both the Austrian and Dutch embassies , though staff at both missions escaped without injury. Ukrainian authorities said Russia fired anti-ship missiles and 98 drones across the country, logging strikes in 18 locations and damaging several diplomatic premises and historic sites in the capital.
Around 10 people were working inside the Austrian embassy when an explosion rocked the area during office hours, deputy head of mission Daniel Ruethlin said, as footage showed workers covering damaged vehicles with plastic sheeting amid the debris. Nearby, the Dutch embassy was hit by a projectile , according to Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, with no casualties reported there either.
Notably, the Dutch mission was struck two days after Dutch weapons manufacturer Destinus revealed that Ukraine had used its arms in recent attacks on the Crimean Bridge, prompting Russia’s embassy in the Netherlands to accuse The Hague of openly participating in the war. No evidence has been provided linking the embassy strikes to that announcement, which nonetheless laid bare the relentless danger facing civilians and diplomatic staff in Kyiv.

Carrying bags and personal belongings, Kyiv residents filed down into the capital’s metro stations to spend the night underground, pitching makeshift tents and laying out inflatable mattresses along the platforms as air-raid sirens warned of incoming missiles and drones. Above ground, a large-scale Russian assault killed at least three people and injured at least 15 , according to updated tolls from Mayor Vitali Klitschko, while damaging residential buildings, a landmark cathedral, bridges across the Dnipro River and the Austrian, Dutch and Brazilian embassies .
All diplomatic staff escaped without injury, though an explosion blew out windows and damaged cars at the Austrian embassy while staff were inside, and a nearby projectile impact caused light damage to the Dutch mission. The barrage came shortly after Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed that Moscow would answer Ukraine’s strikes on the Crimean Bridge with retaliation that would be “much more painful”.
Throughout the conflict, Kyiv’s metro network has served as an indispensable subterranean sanctuary, offering protection to civilians whenever Russian attacks put homes, offices and urban infrastructure in the crosshairs.

Russia launched a major missile and drone attack on several Ukrainian cities overnight
Russia has targeted bridges in Kyiv and killed six during one of the largest air attacks of the war so far, days after Ukraine inflicted heavy damage on the strategically important Crimean Bridge.
Two people were also killed in Russian strikes on a railway station in the western city of Lviv.
Ballistic missiles hit three bridges over the Dnipro River, killing three people and injuring 15 more, the city's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for Ukraine's strike on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.
The three Kyiv bridges targeted overnight - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - have been closed to traffic, adding to disruption created by retaliatory strikes on bridges earlier this week.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary".
He added that an unspecified critical infrastructure facility was also damaged and seven medical personnel were injured during the night's assault.
Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.
Since illegally annexing the Crimea in 2014, Moscow has housed troops and military equipment there, with occupying forces travelling through the peninsula towards the front line.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said an operation to weaken the bridge's defences and ultimately cause part of it to collapse had been weeks in the making.
Russian President Vladimir Putin - who personally opened the bridge in 2019 to international condemnation - said the Kremlin's retaliation for the strike would be "far more painful".
Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.
Ukraine's air force says almost 100 missiles were launched by Russia in its overnight attack - one of the largest attacks since the invasion began in 2022. It also involved around 400 drones.
The attack was "one of the most powerful" yet, according to Yuriy Ignat, head of communications for the Ukrainian air force.
Two people were killed in a hit on the Sknyliv railway station in the south-west of Lviv, the city's Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said.
He shared a picture of the ruined remains of what he said was the station's ticket terminal.
At least two people were killed in a strike on a railway station in western Ukraine
Ten people were injured and a rescue operation at the site is ongoing.
Four people were also injured in Kharkiv after drones struck a hospital and a residential district, according to local officials.

Watch: Burnham says he wants 'best deal for Britain' at UK-EU summit
Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.
The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.
The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum.
A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.
The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.
In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.
Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.
Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.
The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.
Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday.
"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.
"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.
"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."
Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.
The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.
The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next
Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?
The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
An agreement on trade could remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.
The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.
However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.
Burnham has also said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.
Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.
The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.
Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.
However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun , external , said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.
He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Thursday, Badenoch said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but "not trade at any cost".
She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.
Appearing on BBC Breakfast on Friday, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage described the agreement as a "very, very expensive and costly error" and said Burnham has no "democratic mandate to do any of this".
He added that the Labour party manifesto was clear that the UK would not go back towards the single market and asked: "Where is our democracy?".
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey told BBC Newsnight that while he agreed with Burnham on "the harms of Brexit", he did not think the prime minister was "going to go anywhere near far enough".
"We need to go further and faster," he said, including returning to freedom of movement - which Sir Ed said would help tackle immigration and boost the UK economy.

The UK and the EU are poised to agree new deals on trade, energy and youth mobility at a summit in Brussels on Friday, as part of UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's bid to reset ties with the bloc. Burnham – who has said he hopes to see Britain rejoin the EU in his lifetime – argues the deals will help fix some of the damage Brexit inflicted.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the EU's top officials hope to seal deals to ease trade and youth mobility at a Brussels summit Friday, billed as a first step in his push to rebuild ties after Brexit .
Since taking power this summer, Burnham has smashed through the taboos in Britain's toxic debate over relations with Europe – going as far as to float rejoining the bloc one day.
For now the summit with EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa will focus on much smaller steps to help turn the page a decade after the UK voted to leave – while Burnham saves for later the bigger decisions on what could come next.
"It illustrates our new approach. Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges. But being constructive and positive – to deliver a win-win for Britain and the EU," Burnham said this week.
"After the summit, we will initiate a discussion with our EU partners about options for our long-term relationship."
Read more Burnham sets out 'new path' for Britain, vows to seek consensus on ties with EU
On the table in Brussels are three main agreements: a deal cutting red tape for food exports, another linking the two sides' emissions-trading schemes and a third on a "youth experience scheme".
Burnham argues those moves – which were in the pipeline long before he entered Downing Street – will help fix some of the damage Brexit inflicted.
British firms will export to Europe more easily again and thousands of under-30s will be allowed to reside for up to three years in each other's territory for work, study or travel.
But while the mood music at the meeting with EU chiefs von der Leyen and Costa may be much improved, old habits still die hard.
Brussels and London wrangled ferociously down to the wire over the details, with EU states greenlighting the deal package late Thursday night according to multiple diplomats, but a final sign-off still needed from the UK side.
One key sticking point was on pinning London down to a future agreement on cutting fees for EU students at UK universities to the level paid by their British counterparts.
Maros Sefcovic, the EU's veteran pointman on UK talks, insisted the atmosphere had stayed "very positive" – "even if the negotiations are very detailed and sometimes very, very hard".
Burnham pledged not to "re-run" the Brexit debate if he became prime minister but has risked doing just that since succeeding Keir Starmer in July.
Having previously said he'd like to see Britain rejoin the EU in his lifetime, the former Manchester mayor has promised to lay out options that could range from leaving things as they are to entering the customs union or becoming a member again.
The strategy is in part because polls now regularly indicate most Britons regret Brexit and would vote to re-enter the bloc if a referendum was held tomorrow.
It is also reflective of Britain's weak economy, damaged by Brexit, and how much the world has changed since 2016, with Europe firmly behind Ukraine in its war against Russian aggression.
Burnham hopes friendlier EU relations will help build a broad centre-left coalition to win the next general election, not anticipated until 2029.
But the strategy comes with huge risks, not least because his own party – never mind the country – is divided on how to proceed.
For now, the prime minister appears to have tempered his early urgency.
"I'm happy with closer ties but he does need to tread carefully," one Labour MP told AFP, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Burnham's push leaves him open to accusations of Brexit betrayal from the opposition Conservatives and hard-right Reform UK party of Nigel Farage – who will give his own press conference in Brussels Friday.
The prime minister has committed to Starmer's "red lines" on Europe for this parliament, meaning no return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.
But calls to go further are getting louder – with former deputy prime minister David Lammy becoming the highest-profile Labour figure to urge putting rejoining the EU in the party's next election manifesto.
In Brussels meanwhile, there is little expectation the UK will return to the fold any time soon.
"I doubt he'd take the risk of a major step that would be so radioactive," said one senior EU diplomat.
"He'll probably keep on trying to nibble away around the edges to improve ties -- and we are open to have as close a relationship as possible."

Retail sales rose in October, driven by people buying long-life food such as tinned goods and UHT milk, according to official figures , external .
Sales volumes were 0.7% higher as people responded to the government's emergency preparedness "Be Ready" campaign, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.
The campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.
Separate research released last week suggested that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying .
The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.
"Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government's 'Be Ready' campaign," ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said:
"Meanwhile fuel sales have been recovering from earlier low levels, despite pump prices rising again."
The rise in retail sales last month beat some economists' expectations - they had predicted a slight fall - and the uptick came after a 0.6% decline in September.
As well as sales being boosted by people buying essentials, visits to art galleries and clothing purchases were also higher in October.
The boost in sales comes at the beginning of the festive period, which is normally the busiest time of the year for retailers.
Jacqui Baker, partner and head of retail at auditing firm RSM UK, said that "retailers will want to see out the year with some Christmas cheer before consumers batten down the hatches in the New Year as energy costs skyrocket and inflation ramps up further".
Typical energy bills are forecast to go up by £443 per year from January, pushing up the pace of price rises.
Separate economic data released on Friday showed the government borrowed slightly less than economists had expected in October.
Borrowing - the difference between public sector spending and income - was £17bn last month, the ONS said. , external
Although that was £0.8bn higher than October last year, it was below analysts' forecasts of about £18bn.
Interest repayments were £11.2bn - the highest October debt interest figure on record - and £2.8bn more than a year ago.
These repayments have been pushed up by higher inflation, as payments on index-linked government bonds are linked to the inflation rate.
Inflation rose to 3.6% in October, mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices.
Inflation has been driven higher in recent months as the Iran war has driven up the cost of energy and fuel.

Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergencies
Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government issued a warning to stock up in case of a disaster.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said that the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month-on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency.
The surge in sales is a welcome bounce back for the industry after a poor September , which the ONS has revised down from a 0.4% fall to a 0.6% fall, fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter clothing because of unseasonably warm weather.
“Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government’s ‘Be Ready’ campaign,” said Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS.
Food store sales, primarily supermarkets, rose by 0.8% month-on-month, the fastest rate since the 1.4% rise in April.
Textile, clothing and footwear stores reported a 1.5% month-on-month boost. An increase in visits to galleries, and a jump in sales of sports equipment, games and toys, lifted sales across other non-food stores by 3.1% month-on-month, the biggest rise since January.
The total non-food stores category – which includes department stores, clothing, household and other non-food stores – increased by 1.1% month-on-month in October.
Non-store retail sales, primarily online but also sellers such as street stalls and markets, bounced back too, rising 0.9% as a turn in the weather last month drove sales of autumn and winter ranges.
However, sales volumes of motor fuel fell by 2.2% last month, the steepest rate since April, as prices at the pump rose.
“October’s retail sales have exceeded expectations, despite low consumer confidence and growing pressure on household finances from higher interest rates and inflation,” said Erin Brookes, European retail and consumer lead at Alvarez & Marsal.
“Retailers will be feeling optimistic as the sector approaches the critical Black Friday and Christmas trading period, with October’s sales growth suggesting consumers are still willing to spend this festive season.
“Despite this positivity, retailers are caught between increasingly price-sensitive consumers and mounting operating costs.”

Britain makes concessions on youth mobility scheme as negotiations on food and farming go down to the wire
British and European negotiators were closing in on a reset deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.
It is understood the EU dropped its demands at the last minute that its students should pay home tuition fees if they attended British universities in a last minute concession to get the deal over the line.
The UK had strongly resisted EU text on the table committing it to home fees instead of “significantly reduced” international fees, but a compromise was hammered out before 10pm, with a “supplementary agreement” to work out the details within the next six months.
Brussels insiders said the EU had kicked the can down the road and agreed not to mention the tuition fees rate in the declaration, with further negotiations to follow in the next six months.
As talks went into the night, EU sources suggested both sides were on track for an agreement within the next day.
On Friday morning, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham , said the UK and Europe were “stronger together”, adding: “The test for this summit is simple: does it make life better for people in Britain? That is what I will deliver in Brussels today – cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people.”
The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, told the BBC that Burnham’s approach amounted to a “betrayal”. He said: “He’s trying to do it incrementally but it’s perfectly clear that this very very soon becomes a debate about do we rejoin or do we stay out.”
But he acknowledged that for food exporters a deal on agricultural standards would make things “a little bit easier”.
On the eve of a summit in Brussels, the EU was “going into a landing zone” on the question of a British voice in shaping the rules under a food and drink agreement the government hopes to unveil on Friday, an EU source said.
There also seemed to be a compromise by France after a dispute among member states over how far Britain could be involved in shaping policies related to the food and drink deal.
The UK had demanded a “voting” role on some law-making in relation to food standards but France heavily opposed, and London eventually conceded on a point many think was unrealistic from the start. Instead, the UK will be consulted on new food laws, but the details on the level of involvement remain to be seen.
Earlier on Thursday the UK made concessions to increase the quota of EU citizens who could take part in a new youth mobility scheme, agreeing a cap of 100,000, instead of 50,000-80,0000 as previously sought.
It was also agreed to raise the age cap from 30 to 31.The number of young British people allowed to go to the EU under the scheme will be matched but could be higher, with some countries, including Germany, being prepared to take unlimited numbers each year .
With less than 24 hours to go before Burnham was due in Brussels for the summit with EU leaders, the two sides still needed to resolve some sticking points.
Speaking in general terms about the disagreements, another EU diplomat said: “It will go down to the wire. Our feeling is that the Brits have to move if they want a deal.”
A spokesperson for the British prime minister also described the talks as close, saying if an agreement was reached, the government would bring forward legislation, the cutting costs bill, to parliament next week.
At the long-awaited summit, the EU and UK hope to sign three agreements, which are expected to add 0.4% to British GDP , including the highly prized food and drink deal that was a Labour manifesto commitment.
The deal, expected to come into force on 1 March 2028, requires the UK to align with EU rules on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) standards, making Britain a rule taker.
Asked about Britain’s status as a rule taker, No 10 said the Labour manifesto had aimed to build closer ties with the EU, adding: “We were obviously elected on a manifesto that promised to reset the relationship and seek to deepen ties with our European friends.”
According to EU sources, the UK has been pushing to have a formal role in EU committees involved in implementing existing and setting new SPS rules. An EU diplomat said: “They want to be able to shape decisions, not only implementation, but future decisions. That has always been a red line.”
Under the SPS proposal, the UK will agree to dynamically align with EU laws and will have a “voice” but “not be in the room” when laws are drafted.
A second diplomat from a country sympathetic to the British position said the European Commission had proposed an “extremely restrictive consultation mechanism” for the UK.
In contrast, the EU diplomat thought it was reasonable for a British representative to take part in the implementation of SPS legislation affecting the UK. “Of course the UK cannot vote in the council as a non-member state, but we feel that we need to be pragmatic about coordination and implementation,” they said.
The issue proved difficult to resolve because it divided member states. France was perceived by other member states to be the main barrier to greater UK involvement in EU working groups on food and drink laws. “They are super principled on that point,” said a second EU diplomat.
The French government does not agree that it has been the main block, arguing that only a few member states wanted to accommodate the UK.
The issue raises the tensions at the heart of the UK’s status as a rule taker, and would be many times magnified were Britain to choose to enter the single market as a non-EU member state. The precise details of how the UK would be consulted on future food and farming rules remain unclear.
Burnham’s spokesperson suggested there was a UK-EU consensus that there would be no further incremental reset summits beyond the one on Friday until a full negotiation commenced on a longer-term, more stable relationship, such as rejoining the single market.
“After the summit, we will begin those discussions with our European partners about the realistic options for our longer-term relationship,” he said.

At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided- missile startup.
In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history.
His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” Dandzbergs tells WIRED. “A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up.”
In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about “attacking hard problems,” breaking things down to “first principles,” and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war—a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities.
“He’s a pretty exceptional person,” says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. “I’m still somewhat in disbelief that we’re talking about a 16-year-old.”
Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup’s guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the “cost per kill.”
As a young(er) kid, Dandzbergs was rarely in one place for long; his family moved between Latvia, Indonesia, Australia, and Spain. His surfer father, part owner of an insurance company, likes to go wherever he might find the raddest waves.
Early in his schooling, which mostly took place online, Dandzbergs demonstrated a clear talent for science and math. His room started to look like a lab, littered with schematics, robotics, Raspberry Pis, and 3D-printed components.
When Covid struck, Dandzbergs’ family returned to Latvia. His parents enrolled him in Astra Nova, an Elon Musk–linked school where students undergo an experimental curriculum built around lateral thinking and problem-solving instead of rote memorization. Dandzbergs took a class taught by a NASA employee and became fascinated by aerospace engineering. His lab creations became ever more elaborate: a bionic arm, a thermal control system for a model rocket, sensors for a self-flying drone.
Around this time, Russia invaded Ukraine. In Latvia, Dandzbergs started to see military jets overhead, and stray missiles were intercepted at the Russian border. With the sovereignty of Eastern European nations under threat, new defense startups began to pop up across the region. Dandzbergs wanted in.
“A patriotic intention to protect my country, European countries, and Ukrainian and American soldiers, and understanding the future of autonomous warfare—that’s my drive,” he says.
To stretch his technical skills, Dandzbergs started to take part in hackathons, where software and hardware engineers compete to develop the most sophisticated prototype from scratch.
In April of this year, he flew to London to take part in a hackathon held by Unicorn Mafia, an invitation-only group of developers. The prize included $10,000 in cash, a plane ticket to San Francisco, and free legal assistance with O-1 visa applications to stay in the US.
Less than 48 hours later, Dandzbergs and his two teammates, Aleksandrs Tihenko and Kai Yang, had built an AI system that could design hardware circuit boards from natural language prompts, much like how a software engineer might use AI to generate code. Though his teammates are both a few years older, Dandzbergs pushed for them to include even more intricate features in the prototype. “It was amazing,” says Tihenko. “The imagination of Henrijs in the hardware space is just crazy.”
Seeing that they stood no chance of beating Dandzbergs’ group and other front-runners, teams started to drop out of the competition, according to Fergus McKenzie-Wilson, Unicorn Mafia’s director and one of the hackathon judges. “What they built was incredibly impressive,” he says. “No one had ever seen that before.”
When the organizers crowned Dandzbergs’ team victorious, somebody handed him the mic. “I’m 16 years old,” he said.
The week after the hackathon, Dandzbergs and his teammates pitched their circuit board concept to YC. They won a place in the summer program, but Dandzbergs wavered over whether he should drop out of high school. The trio also sparred over whether the startup should focus on applying the technology to the defense sector, Dandzbergs’ primary area of interest. Dandzbergs ended up pulling out of the partnership. “It was hard,” says Tihenko. “But ultimately we just settled that the best decision for the company would be to part ways and focus on different things.”
By the summer, Danzbergs was set on building a defense startup and reapplied to YC on his own. He had spotted a gap in the market, he claimed, for AI-guided missiles that were more precise and could carry bigger warheads than the drones deployed widely in Ukraine. His products, he added, would be cheaper and easier to manufacture than hulking great rocket systems.
YC initially tried to steer him away. Dandzbergs was promising a lot of everything, all at once. It wasn’t clear whether his idea could work or whether pulling out of school was the right thing for him to do. “There’s a paternal element to it,” says Taggar. “You don’t want to be screwing up people's lives—and working on a startup is a pretty serious thing.”
Dandzbergs is up against a fleet of defense companies—from Anduril to CoAspire to Leidos—aiming to develop cheaper, mass-producible missiles. The more sophisticated the guidance system, the more difficult that task becomes.
“You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t go very far. You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t carry much of a payload. You can build a cheap missile that has a low reliability rate,” says Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project and senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “There are trade-offs.”
But Dandzbergs wasn’t going to be dissuaded, and YC figured that somebody else would probably invest in his idea. The incubator invited him to join its fall program. “Big picture, you never know if these things are possible or not,” says Taggar. “Is it a non-zero-percent chance that it could be possible? That’s frankly the threshold, especially if it’s a really big [idea].”
So far, according to Dandzbergs, Polemos Industries has developed the software system that will guide its missiles and has begun to hammer out elements of the hardware design. By the time the YC program finishes in December, he hopes to be able to showcase a prototype missile.
If he does ultimately succeed, though, Dandzbergs will need to confront an assortment of hairy ethical quandaries. Who should have access to these new missiles? What if a technical error were to result in friendly fire? Can he make peace with his technology being used to end somebody’s life?
Dandzbergs claims that he has come to terms with these issues. He says he takes solace in the belief that his motivations are pure: to protect the US and its European allies.
By his logic, autonomous weapons are an inevitable part of the future, so he might as well be the one who builds them. “I choose not to shy away from the emergence of modern conflict as a global issue. I simply don’t have a lot of respect for people that do,” he says. “I want to be part of it. I want to move with the future of warfare.”
But others who have found themselves in a similar position say it’s difficult to know in advance how somebody will deal with the knowledge that their invention has killed people.

Tashima is one of three names on the ballot for the March election, along with current President Infantino and Diallo.
Japanese football official Kozo Tashima said on Friday that ⁠the handling of Folarin Balogun’s red ⁠card at the 2026 World Cup was what prompted him to run for FIFA president against Gianni Infantino.
FIFA suspended forward Balogun’s automatic one-match ban for a red card in July, allowing the American striker to play against Belgium after United States ⁠President Donald Trump said he had personally asked President Infantino to review the sanction.
The decision triggered a swift and fiery backlash and, along with an aborted attempt to sell a stake in FIFA tournaments , led to opposition to Infantino’s re-election as president.
Tashima said he wanted to restore trust in FIFA, drawing parallels with ⁠2016, when Infantino took charge after a corruption scandal .
“Ten years ago something similar happened, and Mr Infantino became president to reform and improve things,” the Japan Football Association (JFA) honorary president told a news conference.
“He has certainly done wonderful things. But in this year, 2026, 10 years later, events have occurred that ignored governance.
“I have worked in football, especially as a player and coach. As such, I cannot accept Balogun’s red card in any way. On top of that, no explanation has been ‌given even now. I felt very indignant about this, and that is why I decided to stand here.”
Following the Balogun incident, FIFA’s disciplinary committee said it had the authority to suspend the one-match ban, and that it operated independently.
FIFA last month said it would amend the rule in its disciplinary code, which had allowed for the reversal of the ban.
The election , set to be held in March next year, will be the first time since he won the post in 2016 that Infantino will face a challenge after being re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023.
French Football Federation President Philippe Diallo also announced a challenge on Monday with the backing of European governing body UEFA . Infantino has the support of Asia and Africa’s ⁠confederations.
“I have not actually received a nomination from any continental confederation. So I’m well aware that I’m at a considerable ⁠disadvantage in this race,” Tashima said.
“It’s a fact that Gianni’s support has been gradually declining. I will keep appealing to voters.”
Diallo said at a news conference on Tuesday that he would reach out to Tashima to “unite forces”. Tashima said he was open to the idea of coordinating with the Frenchman’s team to avoid splitting the anti-Infantino vote.
“I don’t think the French candidate’s ⁠entry puts me at a disadvantage. In fact, France has ties to Africa and other regions, so Mr Diallo’s entry may bring those votes,” he added.
“Watching his press conference, I saw that he pointed out FIFA’s accounting and other ⁠figures in great detail. I find it reassuring that such a professional has joined.”
Tashima is a former Japan international and youth coach and the first Japanese candidate to stand for FIFA president. He has served on the FIFA Council since 2015.
The 68-year-old said that if elected, he would shun the spotlight.
“A foreign media person described me very accurately. They said that if I’m elected, I might become the least conspicuous president ever,” he said.
“That may have been ‌a bit of irony, but I’m fine with it. It’s not the president who should stand out, but the players.”
He added that he would need to be modest in his campaigning, much of which would be funded by his own money.
“The JFA’s budget for this year is already set, so of ‌course, ‌I would like support from the JFA, but we’ll also have to gather funds, for example by creating a fund or running crowdfunding,” he said.
“I won’t spend wastefully. I also have no intention of flying by private jet or anything like that.”

Sean Cairncross is leaving his role as national cyber director after a chaotic week of tech outages. Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, will assume the position in an acting capacity.
Sean Cairncross is exiting his post as White House national cyber director after a series of technology-related outages in the United States over the week led to disruptions in air travel , banking and national security networks.
Shortly after Axios and other US news outlets first reported Cairncross' departure on Friday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the Pentagon's Chief Information Officer, Kirsten Davies, as the new cyber director, congratulating her on X.
"Look forward to working together to strengthen America's cybersecurity," Rubio said.
Davies will assume the position in an acting capacity, media outlets reported citing White House officials.
"Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected," Davies wrote on X late Thursday night, as she thanked US President Donald Trump and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller for their "faith and steady confidence" in her.
"Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future."
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth referred to Davies' tenure at the Pentagon as one in which "she has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional."
"We are confident she will advance President Trump's America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape," the Pentagon chief said.
The Trump administration came under scrutiny in recent days after the US witnessed a major tech meltdown as service outages affected not just travel, communications, and e-commerce, but also the National Security Agency.
Top US officials have since sought to assure people in the country that there was no evidence of a cyberattack.
In 2025, Trump nominated Cairncross to serve as his top adviser on cybersecurity and data protection policy. He was subsequently confirmed to the post by the Senate.

Haitian security forces launched a major offensive on Thursday to retake Martissant, a strategic corridor linking Port-au-Prince with the country's western and southern regions that gangs have controlled for five years. Police said at least 34 suspected gang members were killed in clashes involving a private security task force.
Armed forces in Haiti launched an aggressive operation on Thursday to remove powerful gangs long entrenched in a key corridor that connects the country’s capital to its western and southern regions.
It is the first significant operation in the five years since violent gangs seized control of Martissant, located in the western tip of Port-au-Prince.
Haiti’s National Police posted a video on X stating that at least 34 suspected gang members were killed in Martissant during a fight with police officers working with a task force composed of members from Vectus Global, a private security firm founded by former US Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince.
Local media reported heavy gunfire and explosive drones in the area as Haiti’s police posted a video of armoured vehicles rumbling through the community.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Martissant is located along Route 2, the main road that leads out of Port-au-Prince to important western and southern cities. Thousands of people would travel through Martissant every day before gangs seized control of the area more than five years ago, disrupting the country’s economy as they prevented goods from entering or leaving the capital. Gangs have since charged tolls or randomly opened fire on cars or buses that dare cross through.
Ever since gangs seized absolute control of Martissant, aid workers and Haitian civilians have been forced to take alternative transportation or use rural back roads.
The fight to control Martissant began in June 2021, when gangs from Grand-Ravine and Village-de-Dieu attacked the Ti-Bois gang. Armed men set fire to homes, killed families, destroyed businesses and seized control of Martissant’s police station.
The clashes forced at least 19,000 people to flee their homes and affected some 800,000 people overall, according to a July 2022 United Nations report.
Several years ago, gangs operating between Tabarre and Carrefour would demand some $380 from those transiting through Martissant, according to a 2023 UN report.
Read more Haitians rally behind Bukele as Salvadoran troops battle gangs
Last year, Haiti ’s Center for Analysis and Research in Human Rights noted that ever since Martissant fell, hundreds of public and private institutions were relocated and more than one million people were forced to flee their homes.
As the fight in Martissant continues, a UN-backed gang suppression force also has made recent inroads against gangs in a push to not only displace them but prevent their return.
“Operations are entering a new phase: increasing pressure on gang networks, dismantling more strongholds, and extending control over strategic areas,” the force wrote Thursday on X.
The gang suppression force said it’s working in places including Tabarre in Port-au-Prince and in Haiti’s central Artibonite region, which has come under repeated violent attacks by armed men.
The force said it has come under fire as it advances along Route 5, “removing obstacles established by gangs to isolate communities and control key routes".
Read more Haitian police retake national stadium after two years of gang control
The force said it also cleared and secured a church and school that gangs had been controlling north of Gros-Morne.
“It is about restoring freedom of movement, reopening access to public institutions, and re-establishing State presence for communities that have endured years of gang control,” the force wrote Sunday on X.
Also fighting gangs are some 2,500 troops deployed by El Salvador last month when four of their own went missing after an October 18 attack in Haiti’s capital.
Following orders by Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele , the troops have attacked the main homes of two of Haiti’s most powerful gang leaders, Jeff and Lanmo San Jou, this month. Neither one was killed.
Read more Amnesty urges El Salvador to disclose terms of Haiti troop deployment
Thousands of Haitians poured into the streets of Port-au-Prince and beyond this week in support of Bukele, but experts have criticised the unilateral operations of Salvadoran troops and noted that the use of explosive drones has claimed a growing number of innocent victims.
A small group of Salvadorans are separately working with the gang suppression force.
In late September, El Salvador’s legislature passed a law authorising the participation of that group in Haiti for another 12 months until October 2027. The law was championed by Bukele and overwhelmingly approved by the country’s congress, controlled by Bukele’s party.
The ongoing clashes with gangs continue as Haiti prepares for its first elections in more than a decade. The country hasn't had a president since Jovenel Moïse was killed in July 2021.

Iraqi security forces will deploy ​in the Kataib Hezbollah stronghold of Jurf al-Sakhar, officials said on Friday, under a compromise deal brokered by Shi'ite politicians. Iraq's prime minister ordered a security intervention earlier this week after accusing the Iran-backed militia of smuggling state-owned oil worth ⁠hundreds of millions of dollars.
Iraqi security forces will deploy ​in Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the Kataib Hezbollah armed group, on Friday, security officials told a press conference, under a compromise deal designed to ease tensions with Iran 's most powerful Shi'ite militia ally in the country.
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi earlier this week ordered security forces ​to prepare to ‌move against Kataib Hezbollah, which officials accused of running an oil smuggling network siphoning state-owned oil worth ⁠hundreds of millions of dollars.
Under the deal, brokered by Shi'ite politicians, Kataib members were expected to withdraw to other parts of Iraq , a major oil producer and ally of both the ‌United States and Iran.
Kataib Hezbollah (Battalions of the Party of God), branded a terrorist group by the United ⁠States, has rejected the smuggling accusations. So far, nine senior security and oil officials have been dismissed following an investigation focused on Jurf al-Sakhar in Babil province, a Kataib stronghold about 50 km (30 miles) south of Baghdad .
Any direct confrontation ​with Iran's heavily armed militia allies in Iraq could be risky.
After one of Zaidi's predecessors ordered ‌a similar crackdown on militias five years ago, the prime minister's Baghdad home was hit in a drone strike that authorities described at the time as an assassination attempt.
US President Donald Trump has pressured Zaidi to disarm the militias that have struck US troops and facilities in Saudi Arabia ‌and the United Arab Emirates in solidarity with Tehran since the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran at the end of February. Kataib Hezbollah and other militias have refused ​to hand over their weapons to the state.
Pro-Iranian militias, including Kataib Hezbollah, enjoy a semi-official status in Iraq, which critics say encourages them to act with impunity. A shadowy group with no announced leadership structure, Kataib Hezbollah has thousands of hardened fighters.
It forms ​several battalions in Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), a grouping of armed factions set up in 2014 to fight Islamic State and ​subsequently recognised as an official security force.
Fighters receive state salaries and Kataib Hezbollah members, including some ​designated as terrorists by the US, hold senior positions in the PMF.
While it is technically under the command of Iraq's prime minister as part of the PMF, the group often operates ​outside the chain of command and has defied and challenged government statements calling for an end to attacks on US forces.
Kataib has its own political party, called Huquq, or Rights, with five lawmakers. An Iraqi official report said the group also generates cash through businesses such as construction, housing, trade, tourism and currency exchange, though the group denies this and says it is dedicated to security.
In August, Iraqi ⁠special forces reporting directly to the prime minister arrested the intelligence chief of the Iran-aligned faction Harakat al-Nujaba on accusations of involvement in drone attacks against US interests.
The ⁠detention, which lasted 48 ​hours, triggered threats of retaliation from the group and prompted intervention by senior Shi'ite politicians who helped defuse tensions. A week later, Iraqi special forces arrested four militia members over allegations they facilitated attacks on US interests.

Known today as “Rabbit Island”, Okunoshima drew roughly 200,000 visitors last year , most arriving to photograph the tame animals roaming its coastal paths. Yet behind its idyllic reputation lies a stark wartime secret: between 1929 and 1945 , the Imperial Japanese Army operated a covert chemical weapons factory on the island, erasing Okunoshima from official maps to conceal production.
Today, the skeletal remains of a wartime power plant and former chemical storage depots punctuate the landscape, while the Okunoshima Poison Gas Museum documents the factory’s operations through workers’ gas masks, period photographs and production apparatus.
Museum director Kazuhito Takahashi notes that many domestic visitors arrive knowing little of what transpired on the island, stumbling upon its dark history only after making the trip for the rabbits. Aided by guided tours for students and travellers alike, the striking contrast between the island’s gentle wildlife and its haunting military ruins has turned Okunoshima into an unlikely crossroads of leisure and historical reflection.

Critics accuse populist president of engineering a de facto one-party state in El Salvador.
El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele has officially launched a re-election campaign that critics say illustrates his bid to make El Salvador a one-party state.
Supporters gathered outside the Supreme Electoral Tribunal on Friday as Bukele arrived to register his candidacy for the February elections.
The populist is widely expected to win the race thanks to the huge political support earned by his crackdown on El Salvador’s violent cartels.
However, the launch of the campaign comes after his party Nuevas Ideas used its supermajority in the country’s congress to remove term limits on the presidency and extend the length of terms from five to six years.
Critics accuse the president of consolidating power by removing checks and balances. The Bertelsmann Transformation Index and others accuse Bukele of creating a de facto one-party state.
The 45-year-old has made uprooting El Salvador’s cartels a core part of his presidency and political persona.
“In El Salvador there is total, complete open democracy,” Bukele told the crowd on Friday. “We’re sending a message to the world that El Salvador will never return to the past.”
He has now begun exporting the model. Last month, he sent about 2,500 soldiers to Haiti after four Salvadoran members of a United Nations-backed force went missing. The deployment has been welcomed by gang-wracked Port-au-Prince.
However, many analysts question Bukele’s motives, accusing him of exploiting the crisis on the island nation to enhance his reputation.
“Bukele is running for a third consecutive term after packing the court, rewriting the constitution to his liking and jailing or forcing into exile those who dare criticise him,” Juan Pappier of Human Rights Watch said, according to The Associated Press news agency.
“The absolute concentration of power in his hands has been the defining feature of his administration.”
Last year, Nuevas Ideas used its supermajority in Congress to abolish second-round votes and bring forward national elections by two years, to February 2027.

Woman who waived anonymity says she hopes her case will mean other victims of abuse are more likely to come forward
A woman who was drugged and raped by her husband and strangers he had invited to their family home has been praised for her bravery in exposing the crimes.
The judge in the case and women’s rights advocates said Joanne Young’s courage had been a feature of the trial. Her decision to waive her anonymity and attend court has drawn comparisons to Gisèle Pelicot, who was drugged and raped by her husband as well as dozens of strangers in France. Waiving her right to anonymity, Pelicot said shame “must change sides”.
In a statement outside court on Thursday, Young said the convictions meant “that those who find themselves facing what I have are more likely to come forward, and more likely to have faith in the criminal justice system”.
Saying that she now lived “with a pain that’s hard to put into words”, Young added: “Consent has to come from the person themselves. No one should be able to give it on your behalf, and no one should be able to rely on someone else’s word that you agreed. At no point did anyone ask me for my consent. I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in the future.”
All survivors of sexual abuse are granted automatic lifelong anonymity and only they are able to waive that right. Women’s rights activists appeared outside Winchester crown court for the trial of the men accused of sexually assaulting Young, brandishing banners such as “Shame must change sides” and “A drugged woman never consents”.
On Thursday, four men were convicted by jury of various sexual offences against Joanne Young. Her ex-husband, Philip Young, pleaded guilty in January to more than 50 offences, including raping and drugging his then wife.
Her daughter Alex has also now called for a change in the law on consent to make it clear that third-party consent cannot be used as an argument in a court of law.
She wrote on LinkedIn: “I am calling for the Sexual Offences Act 2003 to be looked at and updated. We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone. We live in a world where someone’s partner can consent for them, and that is enough to use it as an argument in a court of law. This is simply unacceptable.”
Jess Phillips, a former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, has suggested online safety laws should be updated to prevent these cases from happening in future.
The Labour MP for Birmingham Yardley told LBC: “The ability of these men to find each other on websites that you and I could just log on to now – it just means that these cases are going to keep on coming.”
After the verdicts on Thursday, women’s rights groups and others heaped praise on Joanne Young for her bravery. Farah Nazeer, the chief executive of Women’s Aid, said: “We stand in solidarity with Joanne Young – a woman of extraordinary bravery who has chosen to waive her right to anonymity when giving evidence against her former husband, who drugged her and invited other men to sexually assault her.
“Chemical coercion is a horrific crime, one that leaves women questioning their own sense of reality and sanity, just as the men they trust abuse them, coerce them and lie to them. The bravery of women like Joanne, and Gisèle Pelicot in France, have been fundamental in exposing this crime and the men that commit it.”
Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales, praised Young’s “profoundly courageous” decision to waive her anonymity but emphasised that there was “no right or wrong way to react after rape or sexual abuse, just as there’s no right or wrong decision when it comes to reporting it”.
She said: “Survivors of sexual violence and abuse impress us with their courage in millions of ways, whether or not they report what happened to the police … For those who pursue criminal justice, as Joanne has done, reporting to the police and giving evidence in court can call for particular kinds of courage: the tenacity to see a case through to trial, to see the defendant and their supporters in court, and to speak about deeply painful experiences in graphic detail in a room full of strangers. And the strength to carry on with everyday life while waiting for an outcome they can’t control.”
Janaya Walker, a co-executive director of End Violence Against Women, said: “We extend our solidarity to Joanne Young, who has shown incredible courage in this case, including the difficult decision she has made to waive her anonymity. Whilst society may wish to think that such horrors are a total deviation from the norm, they demonstrate the horrifying reality that the greatest danger to women is often inside their own home.”
The Labour peer Thangam Debbonaire told the BBC’s Newsnight the statement outside court was “extraordinary”, adding: “ I feel really moved by her … She is an extraordinary example, and the fact that she has done what she has done, for women, and she said that so clearly, is really moving.”
Young briefly gave evidence in person at the trial, glancing occasionally towards the defendants in the dock. At one point, Mr Justice Saini asked her to keep her voice up. Much of her evidence was given in police interviews that were filmed and shown to the jury.
James Foster, a specialist prosecutor in the Crown Prosecution Service’s Wessex complex casework unit, said: “Joanne Young’s decision to waive her anonymity and attend this trial speaks volumes about her courage and resolve … she sat in court [and] listened to the most intimate and distressing details of what was done to her while she was drugged and unaware.”
Foster said waiving anonymity was an entirely personal decision with no right or wrong choice. He said he wanted to reassure the public that victims of sexual offences retained full entitlement to complete anonymity when reporting crimes.
texts.https://www.dw.com/en/iraq-s-risky-stand:
This week, Iraqi security forces surrounded an area run by the Kataib Hezbollah militia. Onlookers describe it as the most dangerous confrontation between the Iraqi state and Iran-allied militias in decades.
For years, there have all kinds of rumors about Jurf al-Sakhar, an area around 50 kilometers (31 miles) south of the Iraqi capital Baghdad. It is controlled by an Iraqi militia called Kataib Hezbollah, that's closely allied with Iran , and no Iraqi government troops or news media outlets have been allowed inside for around 12 years.
Rumors about what's happening in the area include allegations about secret prisons, mass graves, drone and weapons manufacturing and storage, as well as criminal activity such as oil smuggling. Jurf al-Sakhar is also allegedly a base for foreign, Hezbollah-supporting nationals from Iran , Yemen, Bahrain and Lebanon.
Recently two people — an Israeli researcher and a US journalist — who were kidnapped by an Iraqi militia are thought to have been held captive in this area.
Jurf al-Sakhar previously had an estimated 89,000 residents but after the extremist group known as the "Islamic State," or IS, rose to power in Iraq in 2014, much of the population was displaced in fighting. The area was eventually taken over by Kataib Hezbollah, a militia that had fought IS alongside other armed groups.
As a collective, the armed groups are referred to as the Popular Mobilization Forces, or PMF. Not all of them have pledged allegiance to Iran but Kataib Hezbollah, a Shiite Muslim majority group, has.
In the past 12 years, tens of thousands of the displaced people from here, mostly Sunni Muslims, have not been allowed to return and the area has been described as militarized.
Its name was even changed by Kataib Hezbollah fighters, from Jurf al-Sakhar ("rocky bank") to Jurf al-Nasr ("bank of victory").
But recent events may shake Kataib Hezbollah's hold on this area.
An early November report for the Iraqi government says that since 2021, the group has smuggled hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil, siphoned from pipelines around Jurf al-Sakhar.
Iraq's new government, headed by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, made several arrests based on the report and demanded that Kataib Hezbollah leave Jurf al-Sakhar by Friday, Nov. 20.
Kataib Hezbollah rejected al-Zaidi's ultimatum, with a spokesperson saying the group would not withdraw "not even over our dead bodies."
Al-Zaidi then ordered state security forces to surround the area, while Hezbollah reportedly brought in reinforcements.
Observers have described the standoff as one of the most consequential and riskiest confrontations between an Iraqi government and Iranian-backed militias in Iraq in more than two decades.
"It is a political signal that things will change, that he [al-Zaidi] wants to disarm militias , integrate them into state and claim back the state's authority," Ulf Laessing, head of the Syria and Iraq project for Germany's Konrad Adenauer Foundation, or KAS, told DW. "But it's a minefield and he needs to navigate carefully."
The standoff is also the result of long-running political tensions in Iraq, where the state is torn between its US allies on the one hand and Iranian allies on the other. Both hold sway in Iraq and are considered important relationships.
During Donald Trump's presidency of the US, and thanks to the US and Israel's war with Iran , there's been more pressure on Iraq to disarm Iran's allies inside the country. Al-Zaidi has set a deadline of next June to bring all weapons under the state's control.
The situation in Jurf al-Sakhar became even more tense this week. Al-Zaidi announced a new security plan for the area that involves other members of the PMF, state security forces and the police. Kataib Hezbollah rejected the plan.
"Al-Zaidi appears serious about ending Kataib Hezbollah's autonomous control of Jurf al-Sakhar," Hayder al-Shakeri, a research fellow at the British think tank Chatham House told DW. "Deploying federal forces and now establishing a new security command there shows this has moved beyond rhetoric."
But how dangerous is the situation really? After all, al-Zaidi was actually nominated for the prime minister's job by a political bloc known as the Coalition Framework, or CF — these are the politicians who represent the PMF in parliament. Kataib Hezbollah's political party, Harakat Huqooq, is part of the CF.
And other researchers have been critical on social media, noting that the PMF troops that will be given partial control over Jurf al-Sakhar (should Kataib Hezbollah withdraw) are associated with that group anyway.
But Iraqi news media have also reported that there are divisions inside the CF, and apparently even within Kataib Hezbollah, about how to deal with the current standoff. Reportedly, some senior officials think that parts of Jurf al-Sakhar could be handed to federal forces in a gradual withdrawal, the London-based outlet Amwaj Media reported earlier this week, while some senior members of Kataib Hezbollah would seemingly prefer to hand the territory over to certain PMF brigades rather than to other state security forces.
Late Thursday afternoon, the news agency Reuters reported that, according to three anonymous officials, all parties had come to an agreement that would allow government forces to enter Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday.
A compromise is good because it avoids violence, KAS' Laessing said. "It might not be what al-Zaidi initially hoped for but it's still a political signal."
If it did come to actual fighting, the Iraqi military has more resources than Kataib Hezbollah, al-Shakeri explained. "[It] could probably take Jurf al-Sakhar if the political leadership and security institutions remained united," he said. "But there would be no easy victory. Kataib Hezbollah does not need to defeat the Iraqi army conventionally. It can impose costs through asymmetric attacks, political pressure and its networks inside the state."
How the reported compromise plays out in the coming days, will also impact other Iraqi militias and they will be watching closely. Because "the core issue is whether a faction can continue controlling territory and economic activity beyond effective government oversight," al-Shakeri explained.
"The most likely compromise may be to remove Kataib Hezbollah's monopoly rather than remove the PMF from Jurf al-Sakhar altogether," he continued. "That would still matter if it opened the area to regular state forces, if it protects the oil infrastructure and places security under a clearer government command structure."
It could also lead to displaced residents being allowed back to their homes.
"But if one PMF faction simply replaces another while retaining its own networks and autonomy, then Zaidi has redistributed armed influence rather than fundamentally resolved the problem," al-Shakeri concluded.

İstanbul'da etkili olan sağanak yağış, kentin birçok noktasında su baskınlarına yol açmıştı. Selden etkilenen adreslerden biri de Sarıyer Ayazağa'daki Phoenix Stüdyoları olmuştu. Murat Boz ve oyuncu Demet Özdemir'in de aralarında bulunduğu 200'ü aşkın kişi, stüdyoyu su basması nedeniyle mahsur kalmıştı.
Su seviyesinin yükselmesi ve akıntının şiddeti nedeniyle bölgeye karadan ulaşım sağlanamamış, kurtarma çalışmaları botlarla yürütülmüştü. Çalışmalar sonucunda Boz, Özdemir ve stüdyodaki diğer kişiler güvenli şekilde tahliye edilmişti.
Yaşadıkları zor anları unutmayan Murat Boz, kendisini ve ekibini kurtarmak için büyük çaba gösteren dalgıç polisleri İstanbul Deniz Liman Şube Müdürlüğü'nde ziyaret etti. Şarkıcı, o gün görev yapan ekiplerin fedakârlığını sosyal medya paylaşımında şu sözlerle anlattı:
"Sel felaketinin yaşandığı gün, ekibimle birlikte mahsur kaldığımız yerden sağ salim tahliye edilmemizi sağlayan kahramanları bugün ziyaret ettim. Bize ulaşana kadar bölgede mahsur kalan pek çok insanın yardımına koşmuş, son derece zor şartlarda, büyük bir özveriyle çalışmışlardı.
O gün gösterdikleri çabayı, sabrı ve fedakârlığı unutmak mümkün değil. Kendi canlarını riske atarak başkalarının hayatını kurtarmak için mücadele ettiler. Allah razı olsun. Bugün İstanbul Deniz Liman Şube Müdürlüğü'nde bizleri ağırlayan, o gün de tahliyemizi gerçekleştiren ekibin başında bulunan kıymetli Ertaç Özcan Müdürüme ve bütün dalgıç polis arkadaşlarımıza bir kez daha gönülden teşekkür ediyorum. İyi ki varsınız."

Genel yönetmenliğini Ömer Faruk Sorak’ın, yönetmenliğini İpek Sorak’ın, başrollerini ise Mehmet Günsür ve Devrim Özkan’ın üstlendiği “ Aşk Tesadüfleri Sever 3 ” önceki akşam Paribu Cineverse Kanyon’da düzenlenen galayla ilk kez seyirciyle buluştu. Film ekibi gösterim öncesi basın mensuplarının karşısına çıkıp soruları yanıtladı. Ömer Faruk Sorak, “Şu an çok heyecanlıyız. İzleyenler karar verecek ama ben çok mutluyum. Filmi izledikten sonra insanların salondan güzel bir duyguyla, umutla ayrılacağını düşünüyorum” ifadelerini kullandı.
İlk filmde canlandırdığı Özgür karakterine 16 yıl sonra yeniden hayat veren Mehmet Günsür, “Aynı karakterle 16 sene sonra geri dönmek çok keyifliydi. Özgür’ün 16 sene boyunca neler yaşayabileceğini düşünmek ve o şekilde hazırlanmak çok heyecan vericiydi. Her oyuncuya nasip olacak bir şey değil karakterin 16 sene sonraki halini gösterme şansını bulmak” diye konuştu. Bazı sahneleri yeniden canlandırmanın kendisinde zaman yolculuğu hissi uyandırdığını aktaran Günsür, “Kendimi zaman yolculuğu yapmış gibi hissettiğim anlar oldu. Sanki 16 sene öncesine gittim. Çünkü bazı aynı sahneleri yeniden canlandırdık” dedi.
Serinin yeni hikâyesinde Mavi karakterini canlandıran Devrim Özkan “Aşk Tesadüfleri Sever” serisinin kendisi için taşıdığı anlamı şu sözlerle anlattı: “Ben de bir ‘Aşk Tesadüfleri Sever’ izleyicisiydim. Yıllar sonra bir oyuncu olarak bu hikâyenin parçası olmak benim için çok gurur verici. Böylesine değerli isimlerle aynı sette çalışmak çok güzeldi. Ömer Hocam, İpek Hocam ve bütün oyuncu arkadaşlarımızla harika bir ekip olduk. Umarım bizim hissettiğimiz güzellikleri seyirciye de yansıtabiliriz.” Mehmet Günsür ile partnerliği hakkında da konuşan Özkan, “Mehmet her zaman çok saygı duyduğum ve birlikte çalışmak istediğim bir oyuncuydu. Yıllar sonra partnerim oldu. Onun gibi bir insanla aynı sahneyi paylaşmak gerçekten gurur verici” dedi.
Galada organ bağışına yönelik farkındalık çalışması gerçekleştirildi. Sağlık Bakanlığı tarafından etkinlik alanında kurulan stantta katılımcılara organ bağışı hakkında bilgilendirme yapıldı. Filmin başrol oyuncuları Devrim Özkan ve Mehmet Günsür de organlarını bağışlayacaklarını açıkladılar.
İlişkinin süresi bitti Galaya katılan Ayça Varlıer, 6 yıllık sevgilisi Serhan Aydemir’le ayrılığı hakkında “Çok medeni bir şekilde ayrıldık” dedi. Ünlü oyuncu, “Aşklar neden biter?” sorusuna da “Her şeyin bir süresi olabiliyor. Bu ilişkinin de süresi bitti” yanıtını verdi.
Deniz Can Aktaş gecede sevgilisi Devrim Özkan ’ı yalnız bırakmadı. Çift, gala sonrası düzenlenen partiden el ele ayrıldı.
Hülya Gülşen kendisi gibi oyuncu olan kızı Naz Çağla Irmak’la birlikte poz verdi.

The leaders of Australia and China have held talks on sidelines of APEC summit. Australian PM Anthony Albanese is also slated to meet Chinese Premier Li Qiang.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Chinese President Xi Jinping held talks on Friday, following which Xi hailed a "comprehensive turnaround" in the ties between two nations and Albanese said his country was engaging "constructively" with Beijing.
The leaders met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Forum (APEC) summit in China's Shenzhen.
Xi pointed out to Albanese that they had met four times since the latter became Australia's Prime Minister in 2022.
"I think it is fair to say that together we have brought about a comprehensive ​turnaround in China-Australia relations," the Chinese President said.
Xi also called for enhancing cooperation in agriculture, ​energy, the ‌green economy and artificial intelligence, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported.
The relations between the two countries hit rock bottom under Canberra's former centre-right coalition government, which had called for an independent inquiry into the origins of the coronavirus .
An angry China retaliated by imposing import curbs worth $13 billion (€12.2 billion) on Australian timber, coal, barley, lobsters and wine.
Since Albanese's centre-left Labor party came to power, China has lifted most of its blocks on Australian exports.
But friction in ties has surfaced occasionally on issues such as China conducting a missile test in the South Pacific and Australia tightening a foreign investment screening in the critical minerals sector.
"It is important that Australia continue to engage in a constructive way with China, manage our differences, but not be defined by them," Albanese told the media on Friday.
"What happens in China does matter for Australia," he added.
Albanese is expected to travel to Beijing and meet China's Premier Li Qiang later on Friday.
On Monday, Australia, which is the world's biggest producer of iron ore, called out China's "manipulation" of trade in the commodity over Beijing's formation of a central buying body to purchase ‌ore on behalf of its steelmakers.
A single buyer has increased bargaining power in negotiations with sellers.
Albanese and Li will attend a business roundtable comprising of senior executives from Australian mining giants Rio Tinto and BHP and ​Chinese company executives.

Esra Erol'un sunumuyla ekrana gelen yarışmaya İstanbul'dan katılan, aslen Rizeli 34 yaşındaki Ömer Çakır, 5 milyon TL'lik büyük ödülü kazanmak için kutularını açmaya başladı.
İlk turda 5 milyon TL'lik kutuyu açtırarak istediği başlangıcı yapamayan Ömer, ikinci ve üçüncü turlarda düşük tutarlı kutularla şansını korudu. Ancak dördüncü turda önce 3 milyon TL, ardından 2 milyon TL'lik kutuların açılmasıyla büyük ödül ihtimali giderek azaldı.
Beşinci turda arka arkaya üç mavi kutu açtıran yarışmacıya bankadan 500 bin TL teklif geldi. Büyük ödül umudunu sürdürmek isteyen Ömer, "Tabloda diğer 5.000.000 TL olduğu sürece devam edeceğim" diyerek teklifi reddetti.

Hollywood yapımlarındaki rolleriyle tanınan Lance Broadway'in cansız bedeni, 17 Kasım Salı günü Dallas kentinde bulunan Love Field Havalimanı yakınlarındaki bir apartman kompleksinde bulundu. Yerel polis kaynakları, saat 18.40 sıralarında gelen acil yardım çağrısı üzerine olay yerine sağlık ve güvenlik ekiplerinin sevk edildiğini açıkladı.
Dallas Adli Tıp Kurumu kayıtlarına göre ünlü oyuncunun ölüm nedeni henüz netlik kazanmadı. Yetkililer, olayla ilgili adli soruşturmanın sürdüğünü ve kesin ölüm nedeninin detaylı otopsi incelemelerinin ardından ortaya çıkacağını bildirdi.
Henüz 43 yaşında hayata veda eden oyuncunun sosyal medya hesabındaki son hareketi de yürek burktu. Broadway'in ölümünden 10 gün önce, 7 Kasım tarihinde Instagram üzerinden yaptığı son paylaşımında futbol oynayan yeğeninin fotoğraflarına yer verdiği ve onun sahadaki tarzıyla ilgili esprili notlar düştüğü görüldü.
1983 yılında Teksas'ta dünyaya gelen Lance Broadway, profesyonel kariyerine beyzbol sahalarında adım attı. Amerikan Beyzbol Ligi (MLB) takımlarından Chicago White Sox ve New York Mets formalarını terleten Broadway, aktif spor hayatını noktaladıktan sonra kamera önüne geçerek oyunculuğa yöneldi.
2013 yılında Gerard Butler ve Morgan Freeman'ın başrollerini üstlendiği "Olympus Has Fallen" filminde gizli servis ajanına hayat veren başarılı isim; ardından "Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.", "Lucifer" ve "Colony" gibi dünyaca ünlü dizilerde izleyici karşısına çıktı.

Dallas Bölgesi Adli Tıp Kurumu yetkilileri tarafından yapılan açıklamaya göre Broadway, salı günü ABD'nin Teksas eyaletindeki bir apartman kompleksinin merdiven boşluğunda ölü bulundu. Genç yaşta gelen ani ölümün kesin nedeni ve şeklinin belirlenmesi için başlatılan adli tıp ve toksikoloji testlerinin ise henüz sonuçlanmadığı bildirildi.
Sporculuk kariyerinin ardından kameraların karşısına geçerek yeni bir sayfa açan Broadway, sinema ve televizyon dünyasında da adından söz ettirmişti. Başrolünde Gerard Butler'ın yer aldığı 2013 yapımı aksiyon filmi "Olympus Has Fallen" (Kod Adı: Olympus) ile beyaz perdede boy gösteren eski sporcu, Türkiye'de de geniş bir izleyici kitlesine sahip olan popüler diziler "Lucifer" ve "Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D." gibi birçok televizyon yapımında rol almıştı.
Teksas'ın Bryan kentinde dünyaya gelen Lance Broadway, lise yıllarında beyzbol sahasındaki yeteneğiyle dikkat çekti. Üniversite kariyerine Dallas Baptist Üniversitesi'nde başlayan Broadway, burada geçirdiği iki sezonda rakiplerine neredeyse hiç sayı şansı tanımayarak üstün bir performans sergiledi.
2005 yılında Teksas Hristiyan Üniversitesi'ne (TCU) transfer olan ve çıktığı 19 maçın 15'ini kazanarak büyük bir başarıya imza atan Broadway, aynı yıl Amerikan Beyzbol Ligi (MLB) oyuncu seçmelerinde (draft) birinci tur 15. sıradan Chicago White Sox tarafından seçildi.
Eylül 2007'de Minnesota Twins karşısında en üst lig seviyesindeki ilk maçına çıkan Broadway, 2009 yılına kadar White Sox kadrosunda yer aldı. Aynı yıl tecrübeli oyuncu Ramón Castro'nun da dahil olduğu bir takas anlaşmasıyla New York Mets'e transfer olan başarılı atıcı, New York ekibinde sekiz maçta forma giydikten sonra sezon sonunda serbest bırakıldı.
Kariyerinin son döneminde Toronto Blue Jays ile anlaşan ancak alt lig seviyesinin ötesine geçemeyen Broadway, profesyonel beyzbol kariyerini noktalayarak oyunculuğa yönelmişti.

Meteoroloji uzmanı Prof. Dr. Orhan Şen , İstanbul'da etkili olan kuvvetli yağış ve lodos için sosyal medya hesabından saat vererek uyarıda bulundu. AKOM 'un bugün yayımladığı bültene göre kentte hafta sonuna kadar aralıklarla gök gürültülü sağanak, yeni haftanın ilk gününde ise lodos fırtınası bekleniyor.
İstanbul Büyükşehir Belediyesi Afet Koordinasyon Merkezi ( AKOM ) 20 Kasım Cuma günü için güncel tahminini paylaştı. Buna göre güne 19 derecelik parçalı bulutlu bir sabahla başlayan kentte öğle saatlerinde yağmur başlayacak, termometreler 22 dereceyi görecek. Akşam saatlerinde gök gürültülü sağanak beklenirken sıcaklığın akşam 16, gece ise 15 dereceye gerilemesi öngörülüyor.
AKOM verilerine göre gün içinde metrekareye 10 ila 25 kilogram yağış düşebilir. Lodostan sert esecek rüzgarın sabah saatlerinde fırtına şeklinde, saatte 30 ila 60 kilometre hızla esmesi bekleniyor. Nem oranı yüzde 70 ile 95 arasında seyredecek, deniz suyu sıcaklığı ise 16 derece.
Merkezin uyarısına göre Orta Akdeniz üzerinden peş peşe gelen alçak basınç sistemleri etkisini sürdürürken bölgeye Balkanlar üzerinden yeni bir serin ve yağışlı hava girişi olacak. Pazartesiye kadar aralıklarla sağanak ve yer yer kuvvetli gök gürültülü sağanak geçişleri yaşanacak, sıcaklıklar 17-20 derece aralığında kalacak.
Meteoroloji uzmanı Prof. Dr. Orhan Şen , X hesabından bir paylaşım ypatı. Paylaşımında İstanbullulara seslenen Şen, Avrupa yakasından Anadolu yakasına geçecek olanlara net bir çağrı yaptı. Şen, köprülerin saat 17.00'den önce geçilmesini isteyerek kuvvetli yağışın bu saatten sonra Boğaz hattında ve Anadolu yakasında etkili olacağını duyurdu.
'Bugün İstanbul 'un Avrupa yakasından Anadolu yakasına geçecekler saat 17.00'den önce köprüleri geçin. Kuvvetli yağış bu saatlerden sonra boğaz ve Anadolu yakasında etkili olacak.
İstanbulda lodos bugün öğlen saatlerinden sonra etkisini kaybedecek.''
AKOM 'un haftalık raporuna göre İstanbul'da yağışlı hava cumartesi günü de sürecek.
21 Kasım Cumartesi için gök gürültülü sağanak beklenirken metrekareye 10-20 kilogram yağış düşmesi, sıcaklığın 13 ile 17 derece arasında seyretmesi öngörülüyor.
Pazar günü hava parçalı ve az bulutlu olacak; 2-5 kilogramlık hafif yağış dışında daha sakin bir gün bekleniyor.
Yeni haftanın ilk gününde ise lodos yeniden gündemde. 23 Kasım Pazartesi için lodos fırtınası uyarısı yapılırken akşam saatlerinde yağmur bekleniyor. O gün metrekareye 5-15 kilogram yağış düşebilir, sıcaklık 11 ile 20 derece arasında değişecek.
Salı gününden itibaren yağış beklenmezken termometrelerde belirgin bir düşüş göze çarpıyor. Salı en düşük 7, en yüksek 12 derece olacak.
Çarşamba en düşük 5, en yüksek 14 derece; perşembe ise en düşük 7, en yüksek 15 derece olarak tahmin ediliyor.
